extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, creative-writing students, and general readers learning about writing dialogue
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to write and format dialogue in literary fiction, including its purposes (characterization and internal thoughts), when to use direct or indirect speech, and recommended handling of dialogue tags and narrative interposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue as character presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue is a direct basic method of character presentation and plays an essential role in bringing characters to life by voicing their internal thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Writing Fiction: use dialogue to make characters believable by allowing them to voice internal thoughts; treat dialogue as a key tool for characterization rather than mere exchange of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotation for significant or dramatic events
rubrics_metrics.description: When significant or dramatic events are happening, dialogue can be written in direct quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otherwise, speech can be summarized as part of the narrative or written as indirect speech, which is useful to get to the core of a scene. Choose direct speech for immediacy and drama; use summary/indirect speech for compression or to focus the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue must do more than one thing at a time
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue must do more than one thing at a time or it is too inert for the purposes of fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from William Sloane: make dialogue serve multiple functions (advance plot, reveal character, create conflict, provide subtext) rather than merely convey literal information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpose narrative to situate dialogue (avoid bare dialogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist must interpose on his own account to let readers know how people appeared, where they were, and what they were doing; offering nothing but bare dialogue makes the work like a play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Percy Lubbock: include narrative beats, description, and 'stage-directions' within prose to show setting, physical action, and speaker behavior so dialogue reads as part of a novel rather than a script.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify dialogue with quotation marks and tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue is usually identified by the use of quotation marks and a dialogue tag, such as 'she said'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conventional punctuation and tags (also called identifiers, attributives, speaker attributions) so readers can follow who is speaking; follow standard manuscript/house style for quotes and tags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer using 'said' as the primary dialogue tag
rubrics_metrics.description: Said is the best dialogue tag to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stephen King recommends 'said' as the optimal tag; its unobtrusiveness keeps the focus on the dialogue itself and maintains readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'said-bookisms' and overusing expressive tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue tags other than 'said', such as 'murmured', 'whimpered' or 'thundered', are known as 'said-bookisms' and are considered to detract from the narrative if over-used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cory Doctorow and other commentators argue said-bookisms lead to 'writerly laziness' because they tell the reader how the character is speaking instead of letting the dialogue convey tone and manner; use them sparingly and let content, rhythm, and action show the manner of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-speaker dialogue is a monologue
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is only one character talking, it is a monologue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize monologue as a distinct form of dialogue and treat its pacing, interiority, and purpose (e.g., revealing thought, exposition) accordingly.
